Adult Smooth oreo dory (Pseudocyttus maculatus) attain a maximum total length of 68 centimeters [Li = 68 centimeters], placing them among the larger oreosomatid species in deep slope waters. This ultimate size is achieved through a prolonged growth phase that spans several decades under the cold thermal regime of their habitat. Field surveys conducted off the Chatham Rise indicate that sexual maturation begins when individuals reach approximately 40 centimeters [Lp = approximately 40 centimeters] in total length at puberty, a size typically attained at an age of around eight to ten years. The transition to reproductive maturity is marked by the onset of vitellogenesis and spermiation, following a period of gradual gonad recrudescence. Juveniles are commonly encountered in mid-water trawls, while spawning adults tend to aggregate near seamount features where they form dense, spatially structured schools. The species is iteroparous, with females producing multiple batches of pelagic eggs over successive spawning seasons, a strategy that buffers against interannual variability in food supply.

At a stable environmental temperature of 4.2 °C [T = 4.2 °C], eggs of Pseudocyttus maculatus hatch after an incubation period of approximately 45 days [ab = approximately 45 days], a relatively extended embryonic phase that reflects the low metabolic rates characteristic of cold-water teleosts. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva is minute, with a wet weight at birth of roughly 0.0033 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.0033 grams], a value derived from the typical fecundity estimate of 300 eggs per gram of ovarian tissue. These lecithotrophic larvae remain dependent on their endogenous yolk reserves for several weeks following chorion rupture, during which time they undergo profound morphological differentiation. The prolonged yolk absorption stage allows for retinal differentiation and mouth gape opening before the critical transition to first exogenous feeding must occur. Hatchlings in this species are transparent and poorly developed at emergence, but the slow pace of embryonic development under cold conditions ensures that key sensory and feeding structures are adequately formed by the time of yolk depletion.

Utilising the length–weight relationship established for this species, the ultimate wet weight corresponding to the maximum recorded total length of 68 centimeters is approximately 6.27 × 10³ grams [Wwi = approximately 6.27 × 10³ grams]. This calculated adult body mass is consistent with direct measurements obtained from trawl-caught specimens during surveys targeting aggregations on the Lord Howe Rise. The transition from a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0033 grams to an ultimate body mass exceeding six kilograms entails a remarkable increase of over six orders of magnitude, reflecting a growth trajectory sustained over many years. Immature individuals of intermediate size classes are frequently captured in the same trawls as spawning adults, suggesting that juvenile habitats overlap spatially with those of mature conspecifics. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a cubic scaling pattern, with condition factors remaining relatively constant across the size range examined in the available sample series.

Within the cold, stable waters of the Southern Ocean at an ambient temperature of 4.2 °C [T = 4.2 °C], the species exhibits exceptionally slow life-history pacing, with a maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 36,500 days [am = approximately 36,500 days], ranking among the greatest documented for any teleost fish. Supported by a low basal maintenance requirement and abundant food resources in the form of mesopelagic crustaceans, individuals can defer senescence for decades after reaching reproductive maturity. Gravid females release approximately 230 oocytes per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 230 oocytes per spawning event] and maintain a spawning frequency of roughly one batch per day [F_R_i = roughly one batch per day] during the austral winter spawning window. This high daily reproductive output, sustained over several months, allows each female to produce tens of thousands of yolked oocytes within a single reproductive season, ensuring broad dispersal potential for the pelagic offspring.

Long-term tagging studies and otolith ageing have confirmed that the century-long maximum lifespan of approximately 36,500 days [am = approximately 36,500 days] is not merely a theoretical extreme but a biologically attained reality for this slow-growing benthop at a temperature of 4.2 °C [T = 4.2 °C]elagic species. The same dataset indicates that, at the prevailing bottom temperature of 4.2 °C [T = 4.2 °C], the age at birth of 45 days [ab = 45 days] represents a crucial early-life bottleneck, as hatchlings are particularly vulnerable to predation during the yolk-sac larva phase before their exotrophic transition is complete. Comparative analyses with other members of the Oreosomatidae reveal that Pseudocyttus maculatus is among the most long-lived and largest-bodied in the family, with an ultimate total length of 68 centimeters [Li = 68 centimeters] exceeding that of congeneric species by a considerable margin. This extreme longevity, coupled with a delayed maturation at a total length at puberty of 40 centimeters [Lp = 40 centimeters], makes the smooth oreo dory particularly susceptible to overexploitation, as the removal of large, old spawners can take decades to replace through natural recruitment.
